segments.text: Your Excellency, Paul Kagame, President of the Republic of Rwanda. Your Excellency, President of the Republic of Togo. Your Excellency, President of the United Republic of Tanzania.

Your Excellency, Director General of the International Atomic Energy Agency. Honorable Ministers, Excellencies, Ambassadors, distinguished representatives of international organizations, investors, industry leaders, researchers and partners, dear young people from across Africa. Ladies and gentlemen, many of you have traveled a long way and we are very happy to welcome you in Kigali.

For what is the second edition of the Nuclear Energy Innovation Summit for Africa, NEISA 2026. Allow me first to express my deep gratitude to His Excellency President Kagame for his leadership and his unwavering commitment to Africa's technological and energy transformation. Rwanda demonstrates that with vision, discipline and ambition an African country can become a model of innovation and resilience.
Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, if you really want to see President Kagame's vision in action, please look up. I don't know if you see it. Even the chandelier looks like an atom.

So Africa is living through a historic moment. Nearly half of Africans still lack reliable access to electricity, yet our continent possesses many of the strategic resources required for a global energy transition. Uranium, cobalt, lithium, graphite and rare earth.
Africa's challenge is therefore not one of resources. It is a challenge of transformation. The question is no longer simply how do we electrify Africa.

The question is how do we empower Africa's industrialization, digital sovereignty and long-term growth in a sustainable way. Fortunately, it was said just now, global financial institutions are beginning once again to consider civil nuclear energy within their financing portfolios. Africa must not be an operator of this new energy era.

Like it is popularly said, if countries are not at the table, they risk being on the menu. Africa should not simply aspire to have a seat at the table. Africa must help shape the table itself and that's what we're trying to do at NEISA

Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, Africa's nuclear future in the 21st century will not look like the nuclear industry in the 20th century. Small modular reactors and micro modular reactors are game changers. This technology offers greater modularity, enhanced safety, shorter construction timelines and better adaptation to our electrical infrastructure.

But they also open new possibilities, not only for electricity generation, but for industrialization, clean hydrogen production and the digital infrastructure of the future. And here, allow me to underline an important global signal. The world's largest technologies companies, Microsoft, Google, Amazon and Meta are now investing massively in nuclear energy.

Why? Because artificial intelligence and data centers require enormous quantities of stable electricity. The digital giants have understood one essential truth. There will be no powerful artificial intelligence without reliable, dispatchable and decarbonized energy.
This is also a message for Africa. There will be no African digital sovereignty without African energy sovereignty. But let us also be clear-eyed.
Ambitions are good intentions but alone will not be enough to materialize that future. Financing will remain a central challenge. The cost of the capital remains high.

Projects remain fragmented and many countries still lack the institutional ecosystem required to move from political ambition to bankable projects. Our objective here in Kigali is not simply to discuss nuclear energy. It is to help transform African ambition into credible and investable pathways.

To do so, we must strengthen financing mechanisms, public-private partnerships, regulatory capacity and cooperation. And in this spirit, I'm particularly pleased to announce here that at NEISA, the creation of the Global Coalition for Nuclear Philanthropy led by the Rockefeller Foundation and Temasek Trust. They are joined by other nuclear philanthropists and partners committed to mobilizing capital in support of safe, secure and equitable nuclear energy deployment worldwide.

This coalition reflects a growing international recognition that nuclear energy is not only a technological or industrial issue. It is also a matter of development, governance and strategic sovereignty. Importantly, this coalition recognizes that Africa must not be treated as a peripheral actor in the future of nuclear energy.

Africa must be part of shaping that future from the very beginning. Above all, however, Africa's nuclear future will depend on African talent and that is key. Human capital is our first strategic infrastructure.

Before reactors come engineers, before deployment comes training and before sovereignty comes knowledge. That is why initiatives such as NEISA NextGen, Women in Nuclear, Youth in Nuclear and University Partnership are also so important. And to the young African present in this room, let me say this.

You're not simply the next generation. You're already the generation that will shape Africa's energy future. Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, NEISA will not ultimately be judged by speeches or panels.

It will be judged by the partnership created, the project launched, the investment mobilized and the concrete decision that emerged from Kigali. Energy lies at the heart of sovereignty and sovereignty lies at the heart of Africa's future. Financing remains a challenge but with sustainable financing models, strong international partnerships, build out of institutional capacity and technology such as SMRs, Africa will be able to move forward.

The truth is simple. Without nuclear energy as part of the solution, sustainable large-scale energy abundance and sovereignty will remain out of reach. We have a long road ahead but Africa is ready to embrace this challenge.
Welcome to NEISA 2026 and let us get to work. Thank you.

Your Excellency, President Paul Kagame, the President of the Republic of Rwanda, Excellencies, Heads of State and Government, Honorable Ministers, Your Excellency, Rafael Meariano Grossi, Director General of the International Atomic Energy Agency, distinguished representatives of international organizations, ladies and young men. At the outset, I wish to express my sincere appreciation to His Excellency, Paul Kagame, government, and the people of Rwanda for the warm hospitality extended to me and my delegation since our arrival in the land of Thousand Hills. Also, thank you.

Also, allow me to commend organizers of the Nuclear Energy Innovation Summit for Africa, NEISA 2026, for convening this critical gathering under the theme, Powering Africa's Future, Turning Nuclear Energy Ambition Into Investable Reality. Africa's economic transformation depends fundamentally on reliable, affordable, and sustainable energy systems. Across our continent, growing industrialization, rapid urbanization, expanding digital infrastructure, and increasing demand for manufacturing and mining activities require stable base load power capable of supporting long-term development.
However, in considering future nuclear energy programs, several important issues must be addressed collectively.

First is financing, which still remains a major challenge, and thanks to Grossi, who told us that financing is there, but then the architecture has to be suitable for African countries. Africa needs innovative financing mechanisms, blending financing models and risk-sharing arrangements capable of making nuclear projects bankable and accessible.

Second is regulatory preparedness and institutional capacity, which are very essential. Safe, secure, and peaceful use of nuclear technology requires a strong regulatory system, skilled human resources, effective safety oversight, and adherence to international standards. Tanzania appreciates the important role being played by the International Atomic Energy Agency and other international partners in supporting African countries in these areas.

Third, public confidence and awareness is critical to allay fears of nuclear threats and leverage on its opportunities. African citizens should be aware and fully understand both the opportunities and responsibilities associated with nuclear energy development. Transparency, safety, environmental protection, and responsible governance must remain at the heart of all nuclear programs.

Tanzania strongly believes that regional cooperation is essential for Africa's successful nuclear energy future. Thanks to President Kagame for championing the coordination of the nuclear agenda in Africa. Thank you very much, Mr. President.
Through these partnerships with international organizations and peers, Tanzania looks forward to learning from global experiences and strengthening cooperation in nuclear energy transition.

Now, allow me also to recall the successful African Energy Summit held in Dar es Salaam in January 2025, which brought together African leaders, development partners, financial institutions, and private sector stakeholders to advance the continent's energy agenda. The summit adopted the Dar es Salaam Energy Declaration, which reaffirmed African collective commitment to accelerate access to reliable, affordable, and sustainable energy as a foundation for economic transformation and industrial development.

The Dar es Salaam Declaration recognized further that no single energy solution can adequately address Africa's growing demand, and therefore encouraged African countries to pursue balanced and resilient energy strategies tailored to national circumstances. This discussion here in Kigali seamlessly complements the commitments made in Dar es Salaam by focusing on how emerging nuclear technologies can contribute to Africa's broader energy transition and long-term energy security. Nuclear energy should not be viewed as competing with renewable energy, but rather as a complementing broader effort to build resilient, sustainable, and reliable energy systems capable of supporting industrial transformation across our continent.

Needless to say that this platform provides an important opportunity for Africa to move from ambition to implementation. We must continue working together to create an enabling environment that supports investment, strengthening institutions, and build the technical capacity necessary for long-term energy transformation. Excellencies, talking again of my country, in Tanzania, electricity demand continues to grow in line with the national development priorities under the country's development vision 2050.

Our installed electricity generation capacity to date exceeds 4,500 megawatts, while national demand is projected to reach 8,000 megawatts by 2030 and 70,000 megawatts by 2050. And it is in this context that Tanzania's advancing nuclear energy as part of our long-term strategy to diversify our energy mix and support sustainable economic growth. To guide this effort, we have developed an ambitious national roadmap for nuclear power development to support an additional 1,200 megawatts of nuclear capacity within the next decade in alignment with the International Atomic Energy Agency milestones approach.

We also formulated the National Nuclear Energy Implementation Organization, or we call it NEPIO, to oversee the preparation and implementation of nuclear power program as required by IAEA. And so, in furtherance of the energy generation systems, we are particularly interested in understanding the opportunities presented by emerging technologies such as small modular reactors and micromodular reactors, which are increasingly being considered globally as scalable, flexible, and potentially suitable solutions for developing countries. In conclusion, I wish to reaffirm Tanzania's commitment in working closely with African partners, international institutions, development finance organizations, and the private sector to explore peaceful and sustainable nuclear energy opportunities that contribute meaningfully to Africa's prosperity and energy security.
Thank you very much. Asanteni sana.

I would first of all like to express to President Paul Kagame and the Rwandan brotherly people the recognition of the Togolese people, the recognition for the hospitality, the recognition for the courage of vision, the recognition for this leadership which, once again, opens a path to our continent that others thought impractical. Mr. President, ladies and gentlemen, there are moments in the life of a continent when we are no longer content to observe, moments when we have to decide.

this morning, is one of these moments because the truth is before us. One in two Africans still does not have access to reliable electricity. The African continent represents a growing part of the world's population.

Our cities will continue to grow, our industrial needs will increase, our economies will become more and more digitalized, and all this requires an energy that we can no longer reasonably hope to obtain from the only sources that we mobilize today. Allow me, then, in the time that is given to me, to make three simple remarks, three questions to which Africa and this summit must answer. The first question is that of lucidity.

Are we, today, ready to recognize together that renewable energies, as essential as they are, will no longer suffice to bring our industrialization? In Togo, as in many countries, we believe in the solar, we also believe in the hydraulic, we are already lighting hundreds of villages with mini-grids. But we are also aware that the transformation industries, data centers, artificial intelligence, the African digital of tomorrow, require continuous, decarbonized, competitive electricity in basic electricity. On this ground, civil nuclear is singularly the small modular reactor, and the micro-reactor is no longer a distant option.

It is an option, we say, mature. The World Bank has lifted its historic ban on financing nuclear. The COP and the financial institutions have validated this technology, because it has changed, the context has also changed.
It is now up to us to change our perspective. The second question is that of responsibility. What do we do concretely to make this ambition come true? Togo has chosen modestly to act.

Member of the IEA since 2012, the national law on the safe, secure and peaceful use of nuclear energy has been adopted, creation in January 2025 of our Atomic Energy Commissariat, election to the Council of Governors of the IEA in 2025-2027, and very recently in Vienna, the signing of a new framework of cooperation with the Agency for the next five years. We have also committed to the exploration of modular micro-reactors for areas not connected to the national network. We are ratifying international safety conventions.

We are building, step by step, the institutional credibility that makes a project bankable. Being responsible is not waiting, it is preparing, it is framing, it is convincing, and above all, it is guaranteeing to our populations that African nuclear energy will be born under the sign of absolute safety and transparency. The third question is that of the common demand.

We are together, ready to do what no African country can do alone. Mutualize our regulations, align our standards, aggregate our demands, build, for the first time, an African framework of nuclear financing with development banks, sovereign funds, private investors. Without this framework, the ambition may remain a dead letter.
And above all, train. Train massively. Scientists, engineers, technicians, regulators, jurists.

Our youth, and particularly our young girls, must be at the heart of this adventure. The African nuclear will not be an imported nuclear. It will be a nuclear thought, operated and governed by Africans, at the service of Africans.
Mr. President, ladies and gentlemen, Africa does not ask to be made the world of a technology. Africa offers a partnership. Africa offers a market.
Africa offers an adult vision of its own energy. We have resources. We have uranium.
We have demand. We also have political will. What we still lack are the financial instruments at the level of our ambition.

And an international story that ceases to consider the African nuclear as an improbable or even impossible horizon to recognize what it is becoming, that is to say, a possible, probable and, why not, imminent horizon. So let's make Nessa 2026 the summit where Africa has ceased to debate how to organize around how and when. The summit of the shift between intentions and investments.

My country will take all its part with rigor, with humility, in respect of the highest standards of security, security and non-proliferation, proliferation and a convinced Pan-African. Thank you for your kind attention.

Excellency, my friend Mahmoud Yusuf, former President of the Republic of Niger, former Chair of the African Union Commission, my friend Mustafa Aki, Rafael Grossi, Director General of the International Atomic Energy Agency. Distinguished ladies and gentlemen, let me begin by welcoming you all to Kigali and thank the leaders here present for honoring our invitation and all the work they do for the importance of this topic we are discussing today. In fact, a number of other leaders had intended to be with us but they couldn't make it.

Either they were here last week or they are in some other places attending to some important assignments. I also thank them. But from the outset, NEISA was designed to bring together leaders, experts, and partners to advance Africa's nuclear energy goals.

The strong participation here today reflects a growing consensus that the future of our economies depends on how quickly we solve the energy challenge. Rwanda is pleased to have successfully completed the IAEA's phase one integrated nuclear infrastructure review. We intend to have nuclear energy operational by the early 2030s and this assessment confirms that we are on track.

For Africa, energy is not simply a development issue. It is the foundation of industrial growth and competitiveness. Modern manufacturing, mineral processing, digital infrastructure, and advanced healthcare all depend on reliable power.

The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence and the data driven industries will also significantly increase energy consumption. Countries that cannot meet this demand will struggle to compete. This is why Rwanda considers nuclear energy a critical component of Africa's long-term transformation.

As more countries move in this direction, international reviews and regulatory processes should not become barriers but instead offer the necessary support. For Rwanda, small modular reactors represent the most practical way forward. They are better suited to the realities of most African countries because they can be deployed gradually and integrated into smaller grids at a lower cost.

Renewable energy will remain indispensable, particularly solar and hydro, where Africa has enormous potential. But our economies cannot function efficiently on intermittent supply alone. At the center of this endeavor is the question of investment.

Too often, investors hesitate because they perceive many risks in Africa. We must work to strengthen regulation, ensure consistency, and accountability in order to build confidence and attract long term capital. The international financing environment is also evolving.

Nuclear energy is increasingly recognized as part of the clean energy transition and that creates new opportunities. What Africa cannot afford is fragmentation. If countries work in isolation, progress will be slow and far more costly.

Cooperation on regulation, financing, and regional power integration is essential. This is precisely why NEISA matters. We are moving the conversation beyond ambition to practical coordination and financing mechanisms that can sustain deployment at scale.

Rwanda will remain and will continue supporting these efforts because this is larger than any one country. By 2050, Africa will have the largest workforce in the world. The demographic shift can become one of the greatest economic advantages of this century, if we prepare for it.

In this regard, we are delighted that Togo will host the next NEISA and carry forward this continental momentum. I also, once again, wish to thank Raphael Grossi of IAEA for the kind support to this effort and also for the single-mindedness with which he has focused matters to do with our continent of Africa and how we can continue moving together forward. I thank you very much for your kind attention.
Thank you.

Good morning Madam President, dear friends. One year ago, more or less, we were here, we came for the first time for this conference organized by my good friend Dr Lassina Zerbo, with this idea of bringing together policymakers, but also companies, institutions across Africa, and also from other parts of the world, for what has been discussed. You saw this very nice video, and in Lassina's words, also a good description of what is going on in the world.

So, I think we are very clear that at the present international juncture, the issue of energy, and energy security, and how to facilitate and guarantee for every nation, and in particular in this continent, has become central to facilitate progress and economic growth. Without it, it will simply not be possible. It was said.

The statistics are there. We know the needs, we know the pace and the projected electrification growth in Africa, which is impressive. We also know the gaps that still exist in the continent with roughly half a billion Africans still without the benefits of energy and electrical power.

But the difference is now that we are understanding what are the levers, what are the instruments that may be there for us to bridge that gap, and to improve things. And in that context, nuclear. From the perspective of the International Atomic Energy Agency, which is this organization of ours, the expression of the multilateralism, global multilateralism that exists since 1957, from the perspective of this organization, the issue is not so much to explain, not so much to advocate, but to really establish the connectors that will facilitate implementation of things, real things.

How do we move from understanding that we have a technology, that there are certain gaps, and that this is also possible in Africa? And here is where the activity, Mr. President of the IAEA, needs to be there to facilitate this work. And how do we do this? Of course, there is a normative perspective, which is important. We have the treaties, we have the conventions, we have the meetings where we set the stage for what needs to be done.

But most importantly, I think, is to be here, as we are in every different member state in Africa, facilitating this. One very important thing is how we build capacity. You were saying just now that before sovereignty comes knowledge.

Knowledge is key. And for us to be able, and for you to be able to host nuclear power plants, big or small, we need to capacitate, we need to train, we need to unleash the force of African talent, which is there, but needs to be reinforced. And this is why the IAEA has been helping in all of these training capacity building programs, education programs that are bringing this capacity here, which is indispensable.

Because even in a world where technology has evolved, and now nuclear through small modular reactors can be seen as something that is achievable, that is easier than these big projects that used to define nuclear energy all over the world. We need the capacity to understand, the capacity to handle, and also to produce. It is very important to see that also here in Africa, there are companies, there are startups, there are people who are already working on innovative designs that could be applicable here in Africa and in the rest of the world. So this is one area where we are hand in hand working with you to try to help on that.

Obviously, any good idea in particular, when it comes to energy, needs financing. It was described before. And for many, many years, one very, very thick wall, one very, very distinct red line that separated many developing countries, but in particular here in Africa, from the benefits of nuclear energy was finance.

And this has been a problem that has been plaguing nuclear energy development in many parts of the world. Last year, a page was turned after consultations with the World Bank, and I want to give a shout out to the president of the World Bank, Ajay Banga, who believed that change could be possible. We were able to sign a historic agreement, the IAEA and the World Bank, whereby now it is possible that the doors of international finance institutions open up for nuclear as well.

It is very simple, but it was not happening. When countries came to multilateral banks, development banks, finance institutions, in many cases, believe it or not, there was a prohibition. Nuclear was not to be financed.

And so that was making this gap even bigger and wider, and fairer, if I can say it. But this has changed. And of course, as always, when the World Bank group takes a direction, then the tone and the melody has changed.

And very, very quickly, a number of other institutions, starting with the Asian Development Bank, we signed an agreement in Manila in December, the Latin American Development Bank, and now, of course, I can tell you that we are in a very advanced stage of conversations with the African Development Bank. So we can also bring the possibilities of financing to Africa. The Islamic Development Bank, we do have agreements with them.

So all these possibilities are there. And what this does is the very important psychological and also economical barrier of de-risking is achievable. So when we can have projects that are, the magic word, bankable, then things become possible.
Then an SMRs becomes something that is a real possibility. So this is the other big chapter I wanted to highlight for you, Mr. President, Madam President. The finance is there.

And what is happening, just to explain what these agreements are for, is that when one of our countries, your countries, will be coming to the African Development Bank or to the World Bank proper with an idea of a certain project, then the World Bank will have a partner in the IAEA to turn to, to make sure that the normative, the safety, the security, the non-proliferation package is there to bring this confidence which is indispensable. So this is why we are so happy that we are also turning this page. The existence of important and strong regulators is, again, an area, and I want to congratulate Rwanda because the Rwanda Atomic Energy Board is there and the Rwandan Nuclear Authority is there and they are providing this regulatory capacity which is indispensable.

So as we can see, the elements are finally aligning for us to move from the declaratory. Speeches can be very nice, but what we need is a reality that changes the lives of people out there. And this is what we and this is what you as presidents and heads of state want for your countries.
And nuclear energy can be a part of that. Will it be the only thing? Will it be the thing? No. It is one important element in intelligent energy grids.

We are seeing all over the world problems that are associated with climate, problems that are associated with situations, political, why not say it, geopolitical situations when all of a sudden over-dependence from external sources of energy becomes a problem, become a blocking obstacle for economic development. And nuclear gives us that. So all these elements, I believe, give us an alternative, an option, which is what we really want.

If I may, to conclude these remarks, I'm thanking you, Mr. President, and thanking you for this conference that is slowly becoming a landmark in the yearly calendar of global meetings on nuclear energy. I think it's important to highlight what we have done here in Rwanda since last year when we last saw each other. I think it's nice that when we come a year after an event, we have something to show for.

Since the last time we saw each other, we have been working with Rwandese experts on a national evaluation, which we are going to be handing over to you, Mr. President, today. So thank you for this opportunity. You know that the international community, and in particular our African friends, colleagues, and partners can count on the support of the IAEA every step of the way.
Thank you very much.
